# Copilot Extensions OpenID Connect Support
Date: 2024-09-26

## Status
Pending

## Context
Due to customer requests, and to ease the barrier-to-entry for implementators, Copilot Extensibility is supporting OpenID Connect (OIDC) token exchange. This will allow implementors can present endpoints which take 3rd party tokens to GitHub. Full details on the reasoning and a description of the end-to-end flow can be found [here](https://github.com/github/copilot/blob/main/docs/copilot-api-service/adr/0024-oidc-for-copilot-apps.md).

As part of this implementation, the Copilot API server (CAPI) needs to present OIDC-style ID tokens to extension's token exchange endpoint. As more general OIDC support across GitHub is a desired feature from the Identity team, Copilot Extensibility is hoping to develop this as a joint effort.

### Benefits: Short-Term
Implementing the features within the scope of this document will allow Copilot Extensions to optionally perform [token exchange](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693.html), allowing integrations to recieve tokens that they themselves issued, instead of the GitHub minted tokens they recieve today. This is desired because:

* We would like to be able to use existing integrator APIs when constructing skills. We wish to avoid a world where a company need to maintain two parallel APIs: one for the public and one for GitHub.
* Integrators would like to avoid having to perform a mapping from a GitHub token to a integrator user's permissions for each message called.

### Benefits: Long-Term
There is a desire both among Hubbers and our integrator partners for general OIDC support with GitHub as an OAuth provider. The features that Copilot extensions require today and what future generalized OIDC support require have a lot of overlap: 

* The generation of id tokens
* Signing key support
* The implementation of a `.well-known` endpoint.

Implementing this feature as part of the Identity stack allows these additional OIDC-related features to be built out more quickly in the future. 

## Non-Goals

* SSO data is specifically being left out of the contents of the ID tokens to prevent accidental caching of this information across contexts.
* The tokens generated as part of this effort are ID tokens (tokens what identify who a user is).  Authorization tokens (tokens that say what a user can do) are not affected by or used in this document.

## Decision
A few features will be implemented into `Authnd` to support ID token generation for Copilot Extensions. `Authnd` currently is responsible for generating credentials, and so extending it to also generate ID tokens feels like a natural extension of what the service already does.

### ID Token Format
ID tokens will be defined in the format by the [OIDC Core Design Document](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html). They will be JSON Web Tokens (JWTs). An example ID token generated by the service would be:

```
{
  "typ": "JWT",
  "alg": "RS256",
  "x5t": "example-thumbprint",
  "kid": "example-key-id"
}
{
  "jti": "example-id",
  "sub": "GitHub User ID",
  "aud": "github.app.client.id",
  "iss": "https://github.com/login/oauth",
  "nbf": 1632492967,
  "exp": 1632493867,
  "iat": 1632493567,
  "act": {
    "sub": "api.copilotchat.com"
  }
}
```

These claims are intentionally kept minimal in order to avoid overspecializing the token...the simplier the token is the easier this feature will be able to be adapted for other usages.

Full details of the claims represented in this token can be found [here](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#Claims)

Note that the `iss` field needs to be auto-generated based on the GHES/Proxmia deployment.

### Signing Keys

In order to sign and verify the ID token, `authnd` needs to have access to cryptographic public and private key pairs. While the [JSON Web Algorithms RFC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7518.html) allows support for both RSA and Elliptic Curve keys, we will use RSASSA-PSS (PS256) keys due to their current strength and library support.

The keys will be stored in Vault, and accessed through the Go Vault API.  Scripts will be created in the `authnd` repo to rotate the primary signing key and retiring any secondary keys.

#### Key Rotation

To handle key rotation, two scripts will be created in the `authnd` repo:  One to rotate the primary key and make it into the secondary key, and one to delete the secondary key.  While administrators should be able to run these scripts manually in order to force an off schedule key rotation, the primary purpose of these will be for automation.  Each script should be deployed as a reoccuring [Kubernetes Job](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/), with the "delete secondary" script trailing behind the "new primary" script by enough time to guarentee all tokens signed by the original primary have expired.

### Discovery Document and JWKs endpoint

So that integrations can access the public keys, a pair of endpoints will need to be made available: The "Discovery Document" and the "Json Web Key Set" (JWKS). These will be hosted until the URL `https://github.com/login/oauth/.well-known`.  `tokenz` can be used to see examples of [the discovery document](https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com/.well-known/openid-configuration) and the [JWKS](https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com/.well-known/jwks), and RFCs can be consulted for the for the full description [here](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-discovery-1_0.html) and [here](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7517.html).

These endpoints will be hosted by `authnd`, and served using `dotcom` as a reverse proxy.  This will require `authnd` to start handling traffic from the public internet, although being behind `dotcom` will allow `authnd` to take advantage of `dotcom`'s infrastructure such as rate-limiting.

### IDToken Service
The following service will be implemented into `Authnd`

```
service IDTokenManager {
    rpc IssueIDToken(IssueIDTokenRequest) returns (IssueIDTokenResponse);
}

message IssueIDTokenRequest {
    claims Claims = 1;
}

message Claims {
    sub string = 1;
    aud string = 2;
    act ActorClaims = 3;
}

message ActorClaims {
    sub string = 1;
}

message IssueIDTokenResponse {
    token string = 1; 
}
```

The purpose of the Issue ID token endpoint will be to create an ID token for CAPI (and other GitHub services in the future). Unlike `tokenz` which takes a variable number of attributes as part of the request, we only take a limited number of known attributes here--Given that the attributes we allow in tokens must be in alignment with those in the discovery document, it makes sense to not allow arbitrary attributes from the request.

`Authnd` accepts 3 parameters to generate a token:
* `sub`: The id of the user who will be represented in the resulting token.
* `aud`: The audience with whom this token is meant to be used. As an ID token, the audience is always the integration, so this field will be the integration `client_id`
* `act`: The actor who is actually providing the token. Since this will be coming from CAPI and not `dotcom`, we want to represent this on the token (in the targeted use case, this will be represented by an `act.sub` value of `api.copilotchat.com`.  Note that this value is not required in every situation...in normal OIDC flow (from a call to the `/token` endpoint) this value can be omitted.

Note that the client does not have control over the lifetime of the resultant token...this will be coded as a configurable value into `authnd` to start.  Variable-lifetime tokens could be easily added later if the need arises.

This endpoint will return an encoded and signed JWT as described above.

## Consequences

Implementing these features into `authnd` will obviously result in increased traffic. However, as extensibility is still in beta (and has only been in open beta for about a month) it is hard to guage the future impact. At the time of this writing, the volume of traffic accessing custom agents is negligable, never passing only a few hundred requests per hour. Given that not every extension will implement this feature, and that we will cache the resultant 3p tokens from those that do, `authnd` should not see a noticeable amount of traffic from the generation of ID tokens for the forseeable future.

Traffic fetching the JWKS is harder to guage. We can look at the existing `tokenz` jwks endpoint, which averages about 41.6k requests an hour. If we hope that copilot exentions achieves the same level of popularity that actions currently has, we can estimate a similar load being placed on `authnd`. Luckily, the jwks is easy to construct, so the computational cost of handling these requests should be very low.

## Alternatives Considered

### Extending the tokenz service

Because Actions already has a service designed to mint tokens and serve the discovery document (`tokenz`), it was considered to extend this service instead of adding this functionality into `authnd`.  This plan was discarded for the following reasons:

* `tokenz` serves a lot of additional claims in its token for Actions, and these claims are present in the discovery document.  These claims are Actions-specific and not needed for general OIDC use.
* `tokenz`'s discovery document is at an actions-specific URL, which would be confusing for general OIDC use.
* The Actions team is in Keep-The-Lights-On mode, and does not have the funding or manpower to suppport additional traffic.

### Forking the tokenz service

Instead of redirecting our current traffic to `tokenz`, it was considered to clone the `tokenz` service and modify it into something that meets our needs.  Incorporating this into `authnd` however has the following benefits:

* `authnd` already exists and augmenting an existing service requires less work than the standing up of a new one.
* `authnd` already handles the creation of credentials, so this fits within its scope of purpose.
* If [Stateless Token Exchange](https://github.com/github/authnd/issues/1503) is still a desired feature for `authnd`, there will be a lot of code reuse from this feature (signing key generation, jwks support, etc)

### Discovery Document and JWKS hosted by dotcom

Instead of hosting these endpoints from `authnd` through the load balancer, they could be hosted on dotcom instead, as dotcom already the host for most of the `github.com` domain.  However, we chose to host them on `authnd` for the following reasons:

* `authnd` is already the owner of the public keys.  In order to host the jwks endpoint on dotcom, dotcom would have to fetch the public key info every time from `authnd`.
* The discovery document could be coded on dotcom without tying the two services together, however, updates to the id token schema would involve updating multiple services.
* Hosting these endpoints on `authnd` allows the service to more freely scale apart from dotcom.


### Discovery Document and JWKS connected to the load balancer directly

Instead of using `dotcom` as a reverse proxy to connect to `authnd`, internet traffic could be routed there from `authnd` directly.  However, this comes with the following downsides:

1. Setting up this configuration in `GLB` is non-trivial.
2. `authnd` would need additional infrastructure to handle internet traffic, such as rate-limiting.

Using `dotcom` as a reverse proxy avoids both these problems.  While this does add a dependency on `dotcom`, as long as no transformations are done on the request/response as part of the proxy, this would be easily decoupled in the future.  See [this slack converation](https://github.slack.com/archives/C060TNMQFE0/p1727971408059949) for a more in depth discussion as what lead to this decision.
